12.text: Some fifty years ago syphilis was much dreaded. The Chukchee regard

13.text: it as indigenous, though its name (aˊtal-vaˊɪrg̣ɪn [aˊtal, “Chuvantzy;”¹ vaˊɪrg̣ɪn,

14.text: “substance”]) suggests the tribe who in earlier times were mediators between

15.text: the Russians and the Chukchee, and probably, after obtaining the disease

16.text: from the Russians, introduced it among the Chukchee. However this may

17.text: be, one afflicted with syphilis was regarded as unclean. At home he was

18.text: provided with bedding of his own, with a separate dish and bowl, and was

19.text: kept aloof, lest others should contract the disease. A family having several

20.text: syphilitics among its older members was considered as “subject to shunning”

21.text: (kuˊrg̣u lɪˊn˙yo). Their fire especially was regarded as tainted. They were

22.text: not allowed admission into clean camps, lest the odor of their hearth and the

23.text: shadow of their entrance might prove infectious to their neighbors. Nowadays

24.text: syphilis has evidently decreased; but elderly men and women with deformed

25.text: noses and ugly scars on their foreheads, showing the third stage of the disease,

26.text: are frequently met with everywhere. Even now these are considered unclean,

27.text: though the precautions against them are not observed. The outbreaks of

28.text: syphilis which occasionally occur among the younger people are considered

29.text: simply as a different sort of disease, milder and less contagious.

36.text: the various parts of the country almost every year, claiming scores of victims.

38.text: years ago, and witnessed it myself two or three times among the Chukchee,
